newsitem.title: PERU: Music becomes weapon of love, war in Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Music becomes weapon of love, war in Peru siege.

text.p: From Mexican mariarchis to military marches, Peru's 54-day hostage crisis has become the unlikely setting for a variety of musical duels and entertainment.

While police and Marxist rebel hostage takers have staged a psychological battle via megaphone and loudspeaker, hostages have sung and played to pass away the hours, and relatives have used music to bridge the gap to their loved ones.
"It's like a radio hit parade here," said Reuters photographer Gregg Newton outside the residence. "Every day, it's a different tune."
Longest on the playlists of this musical medley have been the rebel hymns broadcast by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas every day around dawn.

The revolutionary anthems, played through a megaphone as a defiant statement of dogged resistance, were such a publicity coup for the MRTA that police guarding the site decided to stake their own claim to musical superiority in the siege.

In tactics reminiscent of the U.S. siege against former Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega after the 1989 invasion, police began to blast military marches night and day from three huge sets of speakers around the residence in an apparent effort to wear down the rebels' resolve.
Residents of the previously quiet upscale neighbourhood of San Isidro were by no means delighted at these musical treats.
"I don't know what they think they can achieve with this music. The only thing they've managed to do is wake up the whole neighbourhood," said resident Josefina Campos.

The battle tunes, which commemorated famous victories and conjured up the atmosphere of the military parade ground, were also used to accompany a provocative armoured vehicle convoy as it rumbled in front of the diplomatic mansion.
The rebels fired on the convoy, narrowly missing police, and Japan strongly urged Peru to tone down its tactics for the sake of the hostages.
In a bizarre variation on the military theme, the soft strains of patriotic ballads filled the air around the residence over the weekend.
The tradional "criollo" music of guitar-based rhythms, played by police since Friday afternoon, were full of eulogies to Peru and its natural wonders.

In sharp contrast with the musical duels waged by rebels and police, hostages and their families have turned to music as a bond to help them through the long hours of waiting for a solution to the crisis.
Captive Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio waved and smiled as he was serenaded with romantic folk songs from loudspeakers held by his tearful daughter on Jan. 10.

And music-loving Peruvian Deputy Energy Minister Jorge San Roman, who requested guitars be taken into the residence to entertain his fellow captives, was treated to Mexican mariachi music and a rendition of Elvis Presley's "Jailhouse Rock" by family and colleagues on his 57th birthday on Jan 17.

Several evenings during the 7-week-old siege, journalists on duty around the darkened building have heard the eerie sound of singing coming from within. On one occasion hostages and rebels could be heard singing the Mexican folk song "I want to return, return, return to your arms once again," but with the words "to my home once again."

At the suggestion of the Japanese government's task force in Lima, a local radio station agreed to play soothing rhythms to the hostages and also "radio gymnastics" -- tunes to which listeners perform stretching exercises, popular in Japan.
One former hostage said that music was often an ice-breaker when tensions in the residence ran high.
When fuel for the building's power generator ran out, casting the home into total darkness for the first time, the rebels ordered all the hostages to go to sleep.

"But it was seven o'clock. Who can sleep at seven o'clock? So we started to sing songs," recalled university professor Carlos Aquino Rodriguez, released after five days. "We must have sung about 15 songs when someone in another room shouted: 'Shut up we're trying to sleep!' But by that time our nerves had gone."
